quests.partialSentence: I ____ never bought anything from that online store before.
quests.hint: The subject is 'I'; think about the auxiliary verb used to form the present perfect.
quests.explanation: The present perfect uses 'have' with subjects like 'I,' giving 'have never bought.'

quests.partialSentence: ____ you ever returned an item to this shop?
quests.hint: The subject is 'you'; think about the auxiliary verb for a present perfect question.
quests.explanation: Present perfect questions with 'you' begin with 'Have,' as in 'Have you ever...?'

quests.partialSentence: She ____ already tried on three different dresses today.
quests.hint: The subject 'she' is singular; think about the matching auxiliary verb.
quests.explanation: With singular subjects like 'she,' the present perfect uses 'has': 'has already tried.'

quests.partialSentence: I ____ never tasted such spicy food in my life!
quests.hint: The subject is 'I'; think about the present perfect auxiliary that matches it.
quests.explanation: The present perfect with 'I' always uses 'have,' giving 'have never tasted.'

quests.partialSentence: ____ your brother ever cooked a full meal by himself?
quests.hint: The subject 'your brother' is singular (he); think about the matching auxiliary verb.
quests.explanation: Present perfect questions with a singular subject use 'Has': 'Has your brother ever...?'

quests.partialSentence: We ____ already eaten, so we don't need a table right now.
quests.hint: The subject is 'we,' a plural subject; think about the matching auxiliary verb.
quests.explanation: Plural subjects like 'we' use 'have' in the present perfect: 'have already eaten.'

quests.partialSentence: I ____ my phone yesterday, so now I need a new one.
quests.hint: The time word 'yesterday' shows exactly when the action happened, pointing to a finished past action.
quests.explanation: A specific past time word like 'yesterday' requires the simple past, not the present perfect.

quests.partialSentence: I ____ my phone, so I can't call anyone right now.
quests.hint: There's no specific past time mentioned, just a present result of a past action.
quests.explanation: Without a specific past time, the present perfect is used to connect a past action to its present result.

quests.partialSentence: She ____ her laptop three times since she bought it last year.
quests.hint: The phrase 'since she bought it' shows a connection between the past and now, with repeated actions.
quests.explanation: 'Since' often signals the present perfect, used here for repeated actions up to now: 'has repaired.'

quests.partialSentence: I ____ the doctor last Tuesday for a regular check-up.
quests.hint: The specific time phrase 'last Tuesday' points to a finished action at a known time.
quests.explanation: A specific past time expression like 'last Tuesday' requires the simple past: 'saw.'

quests.partialSentence: I ____ this medicine before, so I'm not sure how it will affect me.
quests.hint: There's no specific past time mentioned, just experience up to now.
quests.explanation: Without a specific time, the present perfect describes experience up to the present moment.

quests.partialSentence: He ____ to the gym three times this week already.
quests.hint: The phrase 'this week' is an unfinished period that includes now.
quests.explanation: Unfinished time periods like 'this week' often pair with the present perfect: 'has gone.'

quests.partialSentence: You ____ buy a ticket in advance; you can pay at the door.
quests.hint: Think about something that is not necessary, since there's an alternative option.
quests.explanation: 'Don't have to' shows something isn't necessary, fitting a situation with another option.

quests.partialSentence: We ____ arrive early if we want good seats at the concert.
quests.hint: Think about something necessary in order to get a good result.
quests.explanation: 'Have to' expresses necessity, fitting something required to achieve a goal.

quests.partialSentence: She ____ finish her project before she can watch the new series.
quests.hint: The subject 'she' is singular; think about something necessary for her.
quests.explanation: With a singular subject, 'has to' expresses necessity: 'she has to finish.'

quests.partialSentence: You ____ shout; I can hear you perfectly well.
quests.hint: Think about something unnecessary because the situation is already fine.
quests.explanation: 'Don't have to' shows something is unnecessary, fitting a calm situation.

quests.partialSentence: We ____ reply to this email by Friday, according to the request.
quests.hint: Think about a deadline that creates necessity.
quests.explanation: 'Have to' expresses necessity created by a deadline or requirement.

quests.partialSentence: He ____ explain everything again because no one understood.
quests.hint: The subject 'he' is singular; think about something necessary for him to do.
quests.explanation: With a singular subject, 'has to' is used to express necessity.

quests.partialSentence: The neighbor ____ lives next door always waters our plants when we travel.
quests.hint: We need a relative pronoun for a person, used as the subject of the clause.
quests.explanation: 'Who' is used for people as the subject of a relative clause, replacing 'he/she.'

quests.partialSentence: The app ____ I use every morning tracks my sleep and steps.
quests.hint: We need a relative pronoun for a thing, here an app.
quests.explanation: 'Which' is used for things or objects, such as an app, in a relative clause.

quests.partialSentence: This is the street ____ I grew up.
quests.hint: We need a relative pronoun referring to a place.
quests.explanation: 'Where' is used to refer to a place, such as a street someone grew up on.

quests.partialSentence: The teacher ____ taught me chemistry last year just retired.
quests.hint: We need a relative pronoun for a person, used as the subject.
quests.explanation: 'Who' refers to people, here the teacher, as the subject of the relative clause.

quests.partialSentence: The textbook ____ we use in class is quite old and outdated.
quests.hint: We need a relative pronoun for a thing, here a textbook.
quests.explanation: 'Which' refers to objects or things, such as a textbook.

quests.partialSentence: That's the classroom ____ we had our final exam.
quests.hint: Think about the relative pronoun used specifically for locations.
quests.explanation: 'Where' refers to a place, such as a classroom.

quests.partialSentence: If I ____ the report on time, my manager will be happy.
quests.hint: First conditional uses the simple present in the 'if' clause, not the future form.
quests.explanation: In first conditional sentences, the 'if' clause uses the simple present: 'If I finish...'

quests.partialSentence: If you send the email now, the client ____ it before the meeting.
quests.hint: The main clause of a first conditional sentence uses 'will' plus the base verb.
quests.explanation: The result clause of a first conditional sentence uses 'will' + base verb: 'will receive.'

quests.partialSentence: If we ____ enough time, we'll review the budget again tomorrow.
quests.hint: First conditional uses the simple present in the 'if' clause.
quests.explanation: The 'if' clause of a first conditional always uses the simple present tense: 'have.'

quests.partialSentence: If the weather ____ nice tomorrow, we'll go hiking in the mountains.
quests.hint: Remember that first conditional 'if' clauses stay in the present tense.
quests.explanation: The 'if' clause of a first conditional sentence takes the simple present: 'is.'

quests.partialSentence: If we miss this flight, we ____ to wait six hours for the next one.
quests.hint: The result clause of a first conditional sentence uses 'will' plus the base verb.
quests.explanation: The main clause of a first conditional uses 'will' + base verb: 'will have to wait.'

quests.partialSentence: If you ____ your passport at home, you won't be able to board.
quests.hint: The condition itself is expressed with a present-tense verb here.
quests.explanation: The 'if' clause of a first conditional sentence requires the simple present tense: 'forget.'
